one_liner: Rust crate: branchless SSSE3/BMI2 protobuf-LEB128 varint encode/decode, 2-6x prost and rustc LEB128 on the author's benchmarks.
what_it_does: Encodes and decodes single protobuf-style LEB128 varints (u8 to u64, plus ZigZag signed variants) in Rust, for protobuf/Avro-style serializers. Not a drop-in for prost or integer-encoding: encode returns a ([u8; 16], len) tuple, decode takes a slice and returns (value, bytes_read) or an Overflow/NotEnoughBytes error. Unsafe variants (decode_unsafe, decode_two_unsafe, decode_four_unsafe, decode_eight_u8_unsafe, decode_len_unsafe) read 16 bytes from a raw pointer with no bounds or overflow checks, and decode_two/four/eight decode several adjacent varints in one call.
how_it_is_fast: Single decode is branchless: it reads 8 or 16 bytes unaligned, finds the terminating byte by inverting the continuation bits and taking trailing_zeros, masks the varint with a blsmsk-style trick, then compacts the 7-bit groups either with BMI2 PEXT (when the build script judges PDEP/PEXT fast) or with shift/mask arithmetic. Encode spreads the number into 7-bit lanes (PDEP or shifts), uses SSE2 compare + movemask and leading_zeros to get the byte count, and ORs in the continuation bits with a vector mask. Multi-value decode uses a movemask of the high bits plus a lookup table and PSHUFB to split adjacent varints. The integer type is a generic parameter, so short targets compile to shorter paths.
when_to_use: Rust protobuf/Avro/LEB128 codecs on x86-64 where varint decode or encode shows up in profiles and you control target-cpu.
Buffers that can carry 16 bytes of tail padding, so you can call decode_unsafe or the 2x/4x/8x batch decoders.
Streams of small fixed-type fields (u8/u16) where decode_four_unsafe or decode_eight_u8_unsafe apply; the author reports 8x u8 decode at 896 M/s (i7-8850H) and 1,106 M/s (Ryzen 5 2600X).
Workloads dominated by long varints (large u32/u64 values), where scalar byte loops are slowest.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ code: this is a Rust crate with no C API; look at MaskedVByte, Stream VByte or SFVInt instead.
Non-x86 targets: no NEON and no scalar fallback (both on the README TODO list); the crate will not compile without SSSE3 set via target-cpu.

Data with mostly 1-2 byte varints decoded through the safe interface: an independent Zen 3 report (issue #14, rustc 1.92) got only 151 vs 123 M/s over a naive loop for safe u64 decode and saw application throughput halve after switching.
Generic binaries for unknown CPUs: the native-optimizations feature and PDEP choice are fixed at build time from the build machine's CPUID.
Block integer compression of posting lists or columns: it does single-integer LEB128, not bit-packing; FastPFor, simdcomp or Stream VByte fit that job.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime (build dependency rustc_version; criterion, integer-encoding, rand, bytes for benches)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; no rust-version (MSRV) declared in Cargo.toml
integration.platforms: x86-64 (and 32-bit x86 cfg paths) with SSSE3 required; optional POPCNT, LZCNT, BMI2, AVX2; no aarch64
integration.thread_safety: pure functions with no shared state (from source); not otherwise documented
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same LEB128 wire format as prost and integer-encoding-rs, but a different function API (fixed 16-byte output array, tuple results)

gotchas: The fast numbers are for the unsafe interface: it needs 16 readable bytes after the pointer and silently truncates values too large for the target type; the safe decode copies short inputs into a 16-byte stack buffer and runs extra checks (author's u32 decode: 332 safe vs 483 unsafe M/s).
Before 0.4.1 (commit 'Correctly decode truncated inputs', 2024-09-03) safe decode::<u8>(&[128]) returned Ok((0, 2)) instead of NotEnoughBytes (issue #10); use 0.4.1 or later.

Enable native-optimizations only with target-cpu=native; the build script disables PDEP/PEXT on AMD Zen/Zen+/Zen 2, where they are microcoded, and a separate 'dangerously-force-enable-pdep' feature overrides that.

The benchmark draws uniform random values per type (rand Standard), so nearly every u32 is 5 bytes and most u64 values are 9-10 bytes; real protobuf fields skew short, where the gap to scalar loops is likely smaller (inferred from benches/varint_bench/main.rs).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over MaskedVByte or Stream VByte when you are in Rust and must keep the standard protobuf LEB128 wire format one value at a time (Stream VByte uses its own format); for C++ protobuf-LEB128 decoding the catalogued alternative is SFVInt.
verified_claims_summary: Author-run criterion 0.5 benchmarks with target-cpu=native and thin LTO (rustc version unstated) on an Intel i7-8850H and a Ryzen 5 2600X decode and encode uniform random integers of each width; on the i7 u32 decode runs at 483 M/s (unsafe) and 332 M/s (safe) vs prost 196 and rustc LEB128 191, and u64 encode at 304 vs prost 46. An open third-party report (issue #14, Zen 3, rustc 1.92) could not reproduce the margin, measuring u64 decode at 232 unsafe and 151 safe vs 123 for a naive loop.
status_note: Stale since the 0.4.1 release on 2024-09-03 with issue #14 (Dec 2025) unanswered, but MIT OR Apache-2.0, dependency-free and on crates.io (about 41k downloads, 5 reverse dependencies).
